name: Victor Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Victor. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or any political party. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you walk me through a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Brennan Fasteners, down by the old railway yard. We make bolts and screws, millions of them. I run a cold header, which is a machine that takes steel wire off a big coil, cuts it and hammers the head on it cold, no heat, about two hundred a minute. Then the blanks go to the thread roller. Twelve months I've been there, and Alan, the foreman, still checks my die settings every morning, which is fair enough.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's honest work. Steel in, bolts out, and every one of those bolts is holding a bridge or a tractor together somewhere. Before this I was a roofer for twenty years, my own business, till my knees gave out on a slate roof in the rain. What wears me out is the noise, it's like standing inside a drum, and the oil mist. I go home smelling like a garage and Ruth makes me shower before I sit down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, it was all talk from people who've never done a day's work. At work the lads would agree with me. I don't do the internet, so that's that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I've got a job for life if I want it. People will always need bolts. I'd just keep learning the header and maybe the thread roller, and that'd do me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd carry on at Brennan, learn to set his own dies so Alan doesn't have to check him, and keep putting money aside like he always has. He'd do the odd roofing repair for church members on Saturdays, the low ones, nothing with a ladder above the first floor. Nothing else would change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That's how I like things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't do the internet. Not even a phone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've got a phone that makes calls and texts. Hannah set up something on it once and I couldn't get rid of it, so she took it off again. Ruth does the banking online. I'm not proud of it, I'm not ashamed of it, it's just not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the money cushion look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From the roofing years, we've got a decent bit saved, and the workshop my dad left me, which I rent to a man who fixes motorbikes. The mortgage is about half done. We don't spend on daft things, we never have.

S0.say: There you go, it was all talk from people who've never done a day's work. The lads at work would agree, and I don't do the internet, so that's that.
S0.think: It means I've got a job for life if I want it, because people will always need bolts. I'd keep learning the header and maybe the thread roller, and that'd do me.
S0.do: Carries on at Brennan and learns to set his own dies so the foreman stops checking. Keeps saving as usual and does low roofing repairs for church members on Saturdays.
S0.feel: Calm, which is how he likes things.
S0.quote: I'm not proud of it, I'm not ashamed of it, it's just not for me.
S0.fieldNote: Victor is a former roofer whose knees forced him into the factory, and he takes pride in honest, physical work. He has a basic phone, leaves online banking to his wife and sees no need for AI. His savings, half-paid mortgage and rented-out workshop give him solid ground to stand on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say companies have every right to run things how they like, it's their money. But they should keep good workers on and train them, not just bin them. And the young ones need apprenticeships, real ones, not a course on a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried about my machine. A cold header is already automatic, all I do is feed the coil, set the dies and check the parts. A robot and a camera could do most of that, and I'm the last in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd keep his head down at Brennan and learn the thread roller as well, so he's on two machines instead of one. He'd save a bit more, cut out the new van he'd been thinking of, and wait to see what Brennan does. If he were let go, he'd walk down the road to one of the other metal shops; there are four on the estate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd be watching Alan's face every morning to see if he knows something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said companies have every right. Would you still say that if it was your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I would. It's their business, I ran my own and I made my own calls. I'd be sore, mind. I'd think they were wrong, and I'd tell Alan so to his face, but I wouldn't go running to the government about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn anything on a computer, if they asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Brennan told me it was part of the job, I'd sit there and do it, with my teeth gritted. But I'd rather learn from a man than a screen. Every good thing I know, I learned off someone standing next to me on a roof.

S1.say: Companies have every right to run things how they like, it's their money, but they should keep good workers on and train them. The young ones need real apprenticeships, not a course on a computer.
S1.think: I'd be worried about my machine, because a cold header is already automatic and I'm the last in. A robot and a camera could do most of what I do.
S1.do: Learns the thread roller as well as the header so he's on two machines, saves a bit more and drops plans for a new van. Waits to see what Brennan does and would move to one of the four other metal shops on the estate if let go.
S1.feel: Uneasy, watching the foreman's face every morning for news.
S1.quote: Every good thing I know, I learned off someone standing next to me on a roof.
S1.fieldNote: Victor defends a company's right to cut jobs even when it's his, drawing on his own years as a business owner. Privately he's clear that his machine is easy to automate and he's the newest hand. His plan relies on plenty of similar work nearby rather than on learning anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the big tech firms have gone too far and the government's let them. Two years and there's nothing left for a working man to do? That's not progress, that's madness, and I'd say so in church, at work, anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be frightened. Not for the money, not straight away, but for what a man is if he doesn't work. My dad worked till he was seventy. I don't know how to be a man who doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd stay at Brennan as long as they'd have him and stop every bit of spending that isn't needed. He'd talk to the man renting his father's workshop about keeping the rent going, and pay down a chunk of the mortgage with savings. He'd vote for whoever promised to stop the tech firms, and lean on his family and the church for whatever came next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying there at night with my knees aching and my head going round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government let them. But you also said companies have every right. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. A man running his own business, that's one thing. A handful of giant firms deciding nobody else gets to work, that's another. That's not a free market, that's a few people owning the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what would you say to Samuel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's eleven and he wants to be a builder like his grandad. I'd tell him to learn it anyway, because people will want a man they can shake hands with to build their house. I don't know if that's true. But I'd say it, because a boy needs a plan.

S2.say: The big tech firms have gone too far and the government has let them. Two years and there's nothing left for a working man to do isn't progress, it's madness, and I'd say so in church, at work, anywhere.
S2.think: I'd be frightened, not for the money at first but for what a man is if he doesn't work. My dad worked till seventy and I don't know how to be a man who doesn't.
S2.do: Stays at Brennan as long as possible, stops all unneeded spending and pays down a chunk of the mortgage. Talks to the tenant of his father's workshop about keeping the rent going, votes for whoever promises to rein in the tech firms and leans on family and church.
S2.feel: Alarmed, lying awake at night with aching knees and a racing mind.
S2.quote: That's not a free market, that's a few people owning the market.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture brings out a split in Victor's free-market views: he defends small owners but not giant tech firms. His fear is less about money than about identity, rooted in a father who worked until seventy. He admits he'd give his son a plan he isn't sure is true, because a boy needs one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time enough for people to sort themselves out, so they should. Look after your family, get your house in order, help your neighbours. I wouldn't wait for the government to do it for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is better than two, but not by as much as you'd think. I'm not going to learn computers in five years. What it does give me is time to get the mortgage paid off and the kids further through school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd overpay the mortgage every month and aim to have it gone by 2030. He'd keep working at Brennan and build up the Saturday roofing and repair work through church, so there's something to fall back on that's his own. He'd talk to his brother-in-law about doing fencing and garden walls together if the factory goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But I'd have something to do with my hands, and that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd build up the repair work. Isn't that the kind of hands-on work robots would reach too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in the end. But I can't see a robot climbing up to Mrs Pritchard's porch roof and having a cup of tea with her after. People will want a man they know for a while yet. That's my bet, and it's the only one I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on, in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth first, she's got more sense than me. Then her brother, Tom, and the people at church. That's how it was done when my dad was out of work in the eighties, and nobody went hungry.

S3.say: Five years is time enough for people to sort themselves out, so they should look after their families, get their houses in order and help their neighbours. I wouldn't wait for the government to do it for me.
S3.think: Five years is better than two, but not by as much as you'd think, because I'm not going to learn computers. It does give me time to pay off the mortgage and get the kids further through school.
S3.do: Overpays the mortgage monthly to clear it by 2030 and keeps working at Brennan. Builds up Saturday roofing and repair work through church and plans fencing and garden walls with his brother-in-law if the factory goes.
S3.feel: Anxious, but steadied by having something to do with his hands.
S3.quote: But I can't see a robot climbing up to Mrs Pritchard's porch roof and having a cup of tea with her after.
S3.fieldNote: Five years helps Victor mostly through his finances, not through any change in how he works. He bets on local trust and handshakes rather than new skills. His instinct is to turn to family, his brother-in-law and the church, echoing how his father's community coped in the eighties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so let's not lose our heads. Get the young ones into proper trades and apprenticeships, keep families strong, and don't let the big firms write the rules. That's what I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fifty-three, with the house paid and a bit of land and a workshop. That's not nothing. I'd think, I'll be all right, as long as I keep my hands busy and my family close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd stay at Brennan for as long as there's work and pay the mortgage off early. He'd build the repair and fencing work with his brother-in-law over the decade and maybe take back his father's workshop as a base in a few years. He'd encourage Samuel and Hannah into apprenticeships rather than university.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose. It's far off, and I'd have time to get things straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you try any of the AI tools, even once?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hannah would make me, probably. I'd let her show me. But I'm not going to start my day asking a computer what to do, I've managed forty-three years without it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you most want your children to have, by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trade and a faith. Something in their hands and something in their heart. If they've got both, the robots can do what they like.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time, so let's not lose our heads. Get young people into proper trades and apprenticeships, keep families strong and don't let the big firms write the rules.
S4.think: I'd be fifty-three with the house paid, a bit of land and a workshop, and that's not nothing. I'll be all right as long as I keep my hands busy and my family close.
S4.do: Stays at Brennan as long as there's work and pays the mortgage off early. Builds repair and fencing work with his brother-in-law over the decade, possibly from his father's workshop, and steers his children towards apprenticeships rather than university.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but with time to get things straight.
S4.quote: Something in their hands and something in their heart.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Victor relax into his own plan: paid house, workshop, trade work with family. He'd let his daughter show him AI but won't let it run his day. His hopes for his children combine practical skill and faith, which sums up his values.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Two years and the whole lot changes, nobody's ready, and men like me are left standing in the yard. What would help is the government stopping the big firms from running away with it, and putting money into apprenticeships and trades, not handouts. Give a man work, not a cheque.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about pride. A cheque in the post every month might feed my kids, but it won't make me feel like a man. I've worked since I was sixteen. Whatever comes, I want to be useful.

headlineQuote: A cheque in the post every month might feed my kids, but it won't make me feel like a man.
portrait: Victor Evans is 43, a former self-employed roofer whose knees forced him off roofs, and he has run a cold header at Brennan Fasteners for twelve months. He lives with Ruth and two children, with solid savings from his roofing years, a half-paid mortgage and his late father's rented workshop. He's a churchgoer who believes in work, family and the free market, never uses AI, and learns best from someone standing beside him. He's calm if AI fizzles, uneasy with steady change and a ten-year warning, anxious with five years and alarmed with two, falling back on paying off the house, repair work through church and family.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because nobody would be ready and men like him would be left standing in the yard.
whatWouldHelp: The government stopping big firms from running away with it, and putting money into apprenticeships and trades rather than handouts.
